title: A Palace in Time
hookLine: Heschel described Shabbat as a sanctuary built not of stone but of time
carry: shabbat is a palace built in time
tomorrow: who's really doing the searching, you or God?

lines: WHERE WILL WE DO FRIDAYS NOW?
cards: Saba David's house is sold. On the phone he asked Noa a quiet question: where will we do Friday dinners now? Hold that, because here's the puzzle.
Heschel read the opening chapters of Genesis looking for the first thing the Torah calls holy. You'd guess a mountain, a temple, an altar, a sacred tree. It's none of those.
It's a day. "And God blessed the seventh day, and hallowed it." Why would the very first holy thing be something you can't stand on, build, or sell?

teach.b: Heschel's answer, in his small book The Sabbath, is that Judaism is a religion of time. A technical civilization, he says, pours its effort into space: what we can own, build and point at.
The Torah turns the eye somewhere else. Before any sanctuary of stone, it hallows a stretch of hours.
He called Shabbat a palace in time, and he said the Sabbaths are Judaism's great cathedrals.

teach.h: THE FIRST HOLY THING IS A DAY.
teach.b: That's the fact to repeat tonight: the Torah's first holy thing, in Heschel's reading, is the seventh day. And here's what solves Noa's puzzle. A palace in time can't be sold with a house.

It doesn't get left behind in a move. Wherever the candles are lit and the week is set down, the palace is standing, in a new apartment or a dorm room or a kitchen far from home. Heschel doesn't say places don't matter.
Jewish life has synagogues, homes, a holy city.
But time comes first in the Torah's own order, and time travels.

teach.h: SHABBAT IS A PALACE BUILT IN TIME.
teach.b: So does a table, as long as someone keeps the hour.

how: Shabbat runs from sunset Friday to nightfall Saturday; Jews who keep it mark its start with candles and a blessing over wine and bread, at home or wherever they are.

games.q: what does “holiness built in time” mean?
o: a temple slowly built over many generations
a sanctuary made of set-apart hours, not stone
a holy object passed down through a family

games.q: a palace in time — tap the pairs.
p: God blessed the seventh day, and hallowed it
can be sold; the seventh day can't

s: in Heschel's reading, the first thing the Torah calls holy is a place
it's a day: God blessed the seventh day and hallowed it.
Heschel called Shabbat a palace in time
for Heschel, holy places don't matter at all
he says time comes first in the Torah's order, not that places are empty.

games.q: you're starting college in another state, far from your family's Friday table. what does Heschel's palace in time suggest?
o: the day comes with you: light candles in the dorm, call home, keep the hour.
Shabbat belongs to the family home, so it pauses until you're back.
find the nearest building that looks most like your old synagogue.
games.why: a palace in time isn't tied to one address. wherever the hour is kept, Heschel's sanctuary stands.

practice: Choose one hour this week to set apart. Decide what stays out of it, a phone or errands, and what goes in: a meal, a walk, a person. Say the day and the hour quietly to yourself, as if you were laying its first stone.

wordCard.voice: Holiness built in time: Heschel's reading of Shabbat as a sanctuary made of hours, not stone, which goes wherever its keepers go.

orig.note: Hebrew: and He hallowed (Genesis 2:3), said of the seventh day.

carryVoice: Keep this one: Shabbat is a palace built in time. A house can be sold; the seventh day can't be.
